query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the stability of the high‐temperature BCC state is governed primarily by a composition‐dependent Gibbs free energy difference between the BCC and competing FCC phases. When the alloy is cooled under conditions that permit sufficient atomic mobility, the narrowing ΔG between the phases drives a measurable transformation toward the FCC state; however, rapid quenching kinetically arrests this transformation, preserving the metastable BCC phase.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy homogenized and stabilized in a single-phase high-temperature BCC state.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermal treatments by varying annealing temperatures and cooling rates after the high-temperature equilibration.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed in an inert atmosphere with precise temperature control. The study compares samples that are rapidly quenched (baseline) with samples subjected to slower cooling or extended isothermal annealing at selected temperatures below the high-temperature regime.
generation.structural_mediator: The phase boundary set by the composition-dependent Gibbs free energy difference (ΔG_bcc-fcc) between BCC and FCC phases.
generation.mechanism: At high temperature, the alloy is stabilized in a BCC state by both entropy and the high ΔG_bcc-fcc. Upon cooling, as the free energy difference decreases, thermodynamic driving forces favor a transformation toward the FCC phase if atomic diffusion is allowed. Rapid cooling suppresses diffusion and locks in the BCC structure, whereas slower cooling or prolonged annealing enables the transformation via diffusion-driven atomic rearrangements.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to controlled slow cooling or extended annealing will exhibit an increased FCC phase fraction (detectable by XRD or microscopy) compared to the rapidly quenched baseline, reflecting the thermodynamic push toward phase equilibrium as ΔG_bcc-fcc decreases.
generation.baseline: The as-prepared alloy rapidly quenched from the high-temperature regime, retaining its metastable single-phase BCC microstructure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in the temperature window where atomic diffusion is activated but not so high that the BCC phase is intrinsically stable. Extremely rapid cooling or temperatures well above the transformation range may mask the transformation, while very low temperatures may render diffusion too sluggish for any noticeable phase change.
generation.uncertainty: While the overall role of ΔG_bcc-fcc and atomic mobility is supported, the exact temperature thresholds and transformation kinetics may vary with minor compositional variations or experimental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple samples of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 from a uniform high-temperature BCC state. Divide the samples into groups: one group will be rapidly quenched, and other groups will be subjected to a series of slow cooling protocols or extended isothermal annealing at temperatures below the BCC stability limit. Compare the phase composition of each group.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for quantifying BCC versus FCC phase fractions
Electron microscopy to evaluate microstructural evolution
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to identify transformation onset temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If slow cooling or extended annealing does not result in a statistically significant increase in FCC phase fraction relative to the rapid quench baseline, or if transformation onset does not correlate with the predicted decrease in the Gibbs free energy difference (ΔG_bcc-fcc), then the hypothesis that phase stability is governed by the composition-dependent free energy difference is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: To generate the fcc to bcc martensitic transformation, we adopt the following strategies: (1) to obtain a single fcc phase in the as-annealed state and (2) to increase the thermal stability of bcc phase at low temperature. It is well known that a key parameter for designing metastable MEAs as well as conventional structural alloys which show the TRIP behavior, i.e., the fcc to bcc transformation, is the stacking fault energy (SFE) of fcc. Though the SFE contains a term expressed by a difference in Gibbs free energies between hcp and fcc phases,,, the fcc to bcc transformation is also analyzed by the SFE. In this study, however, we reveal that a difference in Gibbs free energies between bcc and fcc phases can be a critical parameter for the fcc to bcc martensitic transformation. The phase equilibrium and stability were calculated by using a Thermo-Calc software along with the thermodynamic database TCFE2000 and its upgraded version. This CALPHAD approach is much more effective than trial-and-error-based conventional alloy-design approaches consuming a lot of costs and time,. The above results reveal that our design approach based on the difference in Gibbs free energies between bcc and fcc phases (ΔGbcc-fcc) can realize the fcc to bcc transformation in MEA research areas. The fraction of bcc and consequent transformation rate according to the Co content and temperature also well correspond to the thermodynamic phase stability. In this section, we discuss the microstructural evolution and phase stability, varied with the balance of Co and Ni, and their contributions to the mechanical response in detail.

drafts.hypothesis: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is controlled by a competition between the inherent thermodynamic instability of the high-temperature BCC phase and diffusion‐limited kinetic barriers that retard nucleation and growth of secondary phases. In other words, the metastable BCC phase is maintained at high temperature by high configurational entropy, but upon cooling, the thermodynamic driving force for transformation to lower-energy phases (e.g., FCC or intermetallic precipitates) is activated only if atomic diffusion is sufficiently enabled by slower cooling rates or prolonged annealing.
drafts.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature, single-phase BCC state
drafts.intervention: Apply different cooling rates and annealing durations after high-temperature processing to directly alter the atomic diffusion kinetics.
drafts.conditions: Experiments conducted in an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation, controlling for sample purity and geometry; temperature regime from above the BCC stability limit down through the transformation range to ambient; comparison between rapid quenching and controlled slow cooling (or isothermal annealing) procedures.
drafts.structural_mediator: The degree of atomic-scale solute redistribution and the formation (or suppression) of nanoscale precipitates or secondary phases (e.g., local clusters with FCC/intermetallic structure) act as the mediator translating kinetic control into observed phase stability.
drafts.mechanism: At high temperatures the alloy is stabilized in a BCC phase due to high entropy. As the alloy cools, thermodynamic driving forces favor partitioning into lower free energy phases; however, the extent of transformation depends on diffusion kinetics. Rapid cooling (quenching) kinetically traps the BCC phase, while slower cooling or extended annealing allows sufficient atomic mobility for nucleation and growth of secondary phases, thereby altering phase stability.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Samples that are rapidly quenched should retain a near-complete high-temperature BCC phase, whereas samples subjected to slower cooling or prolonged annealing will exhibit an increased volume fraction of secondary phases such as precipitates with FCC or intermetallic structures. The transition in phase composition correlates directly with the available diffusion time during cooling.
drafts.baseline: Rapid quenching from the high-temperature BCC state, which preserves the metastable single-phase structure due to kinetic arrest of atomic diffusion.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies specifically to Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 within the examined composition and thermal range; external factors such as applied stress, accidental impurities, or non-ideal atmospheric conditions are excluded to maintain focus on the thermal history’s effect on phase stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples from a single high-temperature BCC state. Split the samples into two groups: one group undergoes rapid quenching, while the other is subjected to a controlled slow cooling schedule (or isothermal aging at intermediate temperatures) to allow diffusion. Characterize all samples with phase identification techniques such as X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC).
measurements: Phase fraction analysis of BCC vs. secondary phases (via XRD/TEM)
Diffusion profile measurements (using elemental mapping techniques)
Transformation temperature and heat release profiles (by DSC)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If controlled slow cooling or isothermal aging does not result in a statistically significant increase in the volume fraction of secondary phases compared to the rapidly quenched samples, then the hypothesis that kinetic control over thermodynamic instability governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the phase stability of the high‐temperature BCC structure is controlled by a balance between thermodynamic driving forces (stemming from composition-dependent free energy differences induced by Al) and the kinetics of Al diffusion. When cooling from high temperature, sufficient Al mobility results in local compositional fluctuations that trigger an ordering transformation and nucleation of a secondary phase, whereas rapid quenching bypasses this diffusion‐assisted decomposition, preserving the metastable BCC state.
drafts.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy in a high-temperature, single-phase BCC condition.
drafts.intervention: Apply different thermal treatments — specifically, a slow cooling (or controlled thermal aging) versus a rapid quench after holding at high temperature.
drafts.conditions: Samples are held isothermally at the high temperature to ensure a homogeneous BCC phase, then subjected either to slow cooling (allowing sufficient time for Al diffusion and ordering) or rapid quenching (minimizing diffusion-driven transformation).
drafts.structural_mediator: Localized Al segregation and the resulting ordering at specific lattice sites mediate the nucleation of the secondary phase within the BCC matrix.
drafts.mechanism: As the alloy cools, the increased mobility of Al enables its diffusion and local accumulation or depletion, which drives a reduction in free energy via ordering transitions. This results in the formation of secondary phases if sufficient time is available. Conversely, fast cooling limits Al diffusion, preserving the metastable BCC state despite its underlying thermodynamic instability at lower temperatures.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under slow cooling, the alloy will exhibit detectable signs of phase separation or ordering—evidenced by the appearance of additional diffraction peaks or secondary phase features in microscopy—while rapid quenching will largely retain the homogeneous BCC structure. The observed differences in phase fractions directly correlate with the extent of Al diffusion-driven transformations.
drafts.baseline: The baseline reference is the as-cast high-temperature BCC alloy before any post-solidification thermal treatment alters its microstructure.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate under thermal conditions where Al diffusion is significantly activated (i.e., below a critical temperature threshold for diffusion) yet remains kinetically controllable by cooling rate. At very low temperatures, diffusion becomes negligible, and at very high temperatures, the BCC phase is intrinsically stable due to high configurational entropy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple samples of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 and homogenize them in the high-temperature BCC phase. Subject one group to slow controlled cooling (or isothermal aging at an intermediate temperature below the critical diffusion threshold) and another group to rapid quenching. Use X-ray diffraction, scanning/transmission electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive spectroscopy to characterize changes in phase composition, crystallographic ordering, and elemental distribution.
measurements: X-ray diffraction patterns for identification of secondary phase peaks
Electron microscopy images to detect microstructural changes and ordering
Elemental mapping (EDS) to observe Al segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slow-cooled samples do not show any measurable formation of secondary phases or ordering (i.e., no significant differences in diffraction patterns or microstructure compared to the quenched samples) despite conditions favoring Al diffusion, the hypothesis that Al diffusion-driven ordering governs phase stability would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the phase stability of the high‐temperature BCC state is governed primarily by the composition‐dependent difference in Gibbs free energies between the BCC and the competing FCC phases (ΔG_bcc-fcc). The presence of 7 at.% Al lowers the free energy of the BCC phase relative to the FCC phase, thereby stabilizing the BCC state despite the possibility for kinetic transformation toward FCC at lower temperatures.
drafts.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy synthesized and stabilized in its high-temperature BCC single‐phase state.
drafts.intervention: Apply controlled thermal treatments (annealing) at temperatures below the high-temperature regime to vary the free energy difference ΔG_bcc-fcc and to allow the transformation kinetics to manifest.
drafts.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert atmosphere to minimize oxidation, with precise temperature control during annealing. Comparison groups should include samples held at the high-temperature condition (baseline) and samples annealed at progressively lower temperatures where kinetic factors may allow the FCC phase to nucleate if ΔG_bcc-fcc is reduced.
drafts.structural_mediator: The phase boundary between BCC and FCC phases, which reflects the Gibbs free energy difference modified by elemental contributions (notably Al’s ability to favor the BCC structure).
drafts.mechanism: The alloy’s phase stability is dictated by the thermodynamic driving force ΔG_bcc-fcc that is composition-dependent. In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the moderate Al content shifts the balance in favor of the BCC phase at high temperatures. However, during cooling or under prolonged isothermal holds at lower temperatures, if the free energy difference is reduced and kinetic barriers (such as sluggish diffusion) are overcome, a transformation toward the FCC phase can occur. Thus, the competition between the thermodynamic driving force and the kinetic limitations governs the observed phase stability.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under controlled thermal treatments at sub–high-temperature regimes, a measurable increase in the FCC phase fraction (detected via XRD or microscopy) will occur if the driving force ΔG_bcc-fcc is reduced enough to allow transformation. In contrast, samples maintained at the high-temperature condition should retain a predominantly BCC phase.
drafts.baseline: The as-prepared Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy in a high-temperature single-phase BCC state, with no significant FCC phase present.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies within the temperature regime where thermodynamic calculations predict a crossover in phase stability (i.e., temperatures below the original high-temperature BCC stability range) and under conditions where the kinetics of phase transformation are not completely frozen. If the cooling rate is too rapid or if temperatures remain well above the critical threshold, the kinetic window to observe transformation may be lost.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple samples of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 and subject them to isothermal annealing treatments at controlled temperatures below the high-temperature BCC stability range. Use identical processing conditions (same atmosphere, heating/cooling rates) but vary the annealing temperature to modulate ΔG_bcc-fcc. Characterize the phase fractions using X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy.
measurements: Phase fraction of BCC versus FCC (via XRD peak analysis)
Microstructural evolution by scanning/transmission electron microscopy
Thermal analysis (e.g., DSC) to capture transformation onset temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under conditions predicted to lower ΔG_bcc-fcc (i.e., at lower annealing temperatures), there is no statistically significant increase in the FCC phase fraction relative to the baseline sample, or if the phase transformation kinetics do not correlate with the calculated thermodynamic driving force, then the hypothesis that ΔG_bcc-fcc governs the phase stability is refuted.

drafts.hypothesis: The phase stability of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in its high‐temperature BCC state is primarily governed by the composition‐dependent difference in Gibbs free energy between the BCC and the competing FCC phases (ΔG_bcc-fcc). In this system, the specific elemental proportions (notably the levels of Cr and Al along with Co, Fe, and Ni) set the mixing enthalpy and configurational entropy such that the free energy difference is minimized at high temperatures, favoring a metastable BCC state. Under thermal treatments that allow kinetics to play a stronger role, this free energy difference can drive a transformation toward a more stable FCC state.
drafts.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy initially homogenized and stabilized in a high-temperature BCC state.
drafts.intervention: Apply controlled thermal treatments (e.g., isothermal annealing at high temperatures and varying cooling rates) to modify the thermal history and allow kinetic effects to emerge.
drafts.conditions: Experiments conducted in an inert atmosphere at temperatures above ~900°C with subsequent cooling at different rates (rapid quench vs. slow cooling) to probe kinetic influence.
drafts.structural_mediator: The relative phase fractions (BCC vs FCC), defect densities, and possible incipient chemical ordering that mediate the transformation.
drafts.mechanism: The alloy’s specific composition sets the contributions to the mixing enthalpy and configurational entropy, thereby modulating the Gibbs free energy difference (ΔG_bcc-fcc) between the high-temperature BCC phase and the lower-temperature FCC phase. Under rapid cooling, kinetic barriers preserve the high-temperature metastable BCC state, while longer annealing or slower cooling allows sufficient atomic mobility for the system to gradually approach thermodynamic equilibrium and transform partially or fully into the FCC structure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: When the alloy is subjected to different thermal histories, one should observe that slower cooling or extended high-temperature annealing yields an increased fraction of the FCC phase compared to a baseline rapid quench that preserves the BCC state. The measured phase fractions (by XRD) should correlate with the predicted shifts in ΔG_bcc-fcc.
drafts.baseline: Samples processed by rapid quenching from the high-temperature regime, retaining predominantly the BCC phase.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to apply within the temperature regime and processing conditions where thermodynamic driving force (ΔG_bcc-fcc) is the major factor. It may not hold if extrinsic kinetic barriers, extreme non-equilibrium processing, or additional ordering effects dominate the phase evolution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple batches of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples and subject them to a series of thermal treatments varying in annealing time and cooling rate. Use a rapid quench to establish a baseline high-temperature BCC state and compare it against samples slowly cooled or held isothermally to promote kinetic completion. Measure the phase fractions via X-ray diffraction (XRD) and perform differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to detect transformation energetics.
measurements: Phase fraction and identification of BCC and FCC phases (using XRD)
Transformation onset temperatures and enthalpy changes (using DSC)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If variation in thermal history (longer annealing or slower cooling) does not result in a systematic increase in the FCC phase fraction (or corresponding changes in transformation energetics) relative to the baseline rapid-quench BCC state, then the hypothesis that ΔG_bcc-fcc governs phase stability would be falsified.
